solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Get on European service to return

indicators.note: to return means to go back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: the RAF (Royal Air Force) is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A traveller boards a European flight or train for the trip home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns ERAF back to front. 'Get on' is the verb sense, as in 'How did you get on?'
explanation.definitionFit: To fare is to manage or progress, as in 'how did you fare?', which is how one gets on.

clue.text: Feature of expert in opposition

parts.note: a facet is an aspect or feature
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: Part of a specialist's role is being on the opposing side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature of' is not a phrase but FACET followed by OF as written.
explanation.definitionFit: People meeting eye to eye are confronting each other, directly opposed.

clue.text: Filling in maestro's informal application for cellist

indicators.note: the filling of something sits inside it, so the letters are found within these words

explanation.surface: A conductor fills in casually for a cellist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling in' looks like standing in, but it points to letters inside MAESTRO'S INFORMAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosin is the resin rubbed on a bow so it grips the strings.

clue.text: Irish cop ordered to arrest doctor with similar appearance

indicators.note: to arrest is to take someone in, so one piece is held inside the other
the letters of these two words are put in a new order, rearranged

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer, a common crossword doctor

explanation.surface: A Garda officer under orders detains a doctor who looks like someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges the policeman's letters into ISORPHIC, and 'to arrest' holds the doctor inside. 'Irish cop' looks like a description but is pure anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Isomorphic things share the same form or structure, so they look alike.

clue.text: Old sailor preferred dealing with explosive ingredient

parts.note: an old salt is a veteran seaman
a pet project or theory is a favoured, preferred one
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A veteran seaman favoured handling gunpowder components.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Latin-derived 'concerning', as in letter headings.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium nitrate is a key component of gunpowder.

clue.text: The writer's keeping a note cordial

indicators.note: keeping means holding something within

parts.note: the setter's own, so my
te is a note in tonic sol-fa, also spelt ti

explanation.surface: An author holds on to a friendly letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cordial' looks like a drink but means friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone matey is friendly and warm in manner, as cordial people are.

clue.text: Pity he's left here gloomy, having lost second round

indicators.note: if he has left a place he is no longer in it, so those letters go

parts.note: taken as the word here
the word he, from he is

indicators.note: having lost the second one means the later of two matching letters is dropped

parts.note: morose means gloomy
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: It is sad that a man has left this miserable place after losing a second bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' makes RE (here without he); 'having lost second' drops the later of the two O letters from the gloomy word, leaving MORSE. 'Pity' is in its older sense of sorrowful compassion.
explanation.definitionFit: In older usage pity meant compassion or sorrow, close to regret felt over a wrong.

clue.text: Home Office head blocking just over 100 ordinary folk

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for the Home Office, the UK interior ministry

indicators.note: blocking means sitting in the way, inside

parts.note: 101 written as Roman I, then O for zero, then I, gives IOI
the poll is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: A senior civil servant obstructs about a hundred members of the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 101 is written as Roman I, zero as O, then I again; 'blocking' sets the old word for head in the middle of that. 'head' is not a leader here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek phrase means 'the many', the common people or masses.

clue.text: Compare entertaining ambassador and cook

indicators.note: entertaining a guest means having them inside

parts.note: cf is the abbreviation for compare, from Latin confer
HE is His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: Judge an envoy's hospitality against that of a cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compare' looks like a verb but is the abbreviation CF.
explanation.definitionFit: A chef is a professional cook in a kitchen.

clue.text: Force state briefly to give up

parts.note: F is the physics symbol for force

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, losing the last letter

parts.note: Oregon is a US state

explanation.surface: Power over a state is about to be surrendered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' clips the N off OREGON.
explanation.definitionFit: To forego, or forgo, is to do without or renounce something.

clue.text: Person in suit beginning to try stew

indicators.note: the word in tells us one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a lawsuit is a legal case
a soul is a person, as in 'not a soul in sight'

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone in a suit starts to sample a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' looks like clothing but is a lawsuit; 'in' sets the person inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassoulet is a slow-cooked French dish of beans and meats, a kind of stew.

clue.text: Crop one stored in old prison

indicators.note: something stored in a place is kept inside it

parts.note: the Maze was a prison in Northern Ireland, closed in 2000
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A harvest is kept in a disused jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The Maze was a high-security prison near Belfast, Northern Ireland, now closed, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize, or corn, is a cereal grown widely on farms as a crop.

clue.text: Perfect maybe on horseback? Don't relax

parts.note: the perfect is a grammatical tense, and 'maybe' marks it as one example
a rider on horseback is said to be up, as in a jockey being up

explanation.surface: A rider is told to keep alert in the saddle rather than slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' is the grammar term, an example of a tense, not praise; a jockey who is riding is 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tense up is to stiffen the muscles, the opposite of loosening, so the instruction fits as an imperative.

clue.text: Feel uneasy about importing a plant

indicators.note: importing means bringing something in, so a piece goes inside
about here means turned around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to worry is to feel uneasy

explanation.surface: Someone frets about bringing in a plant from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns WORRY into YRROW, and 'importing' puts A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrow is a common flowering herb, Achillea, with feathery leaves.

clue.text: Carriage with frivolous warning to driver behind

parts.note: a brake is a horse-drawn carriage, as in shooting brake
light means frivolous, as in light reading

explanation.surface: A playful coach signals to the vehicle following.
explanation.walkthrough: A brake was a large horse-drawn wagon, the root of 'shooting brake' for an estate car.
explanation.definitionFit: The red lamp at the back of a car glows when slowing, alerting traffic following.

clue.text: Supporter of the Reds on the same train as me?

definitions.meaning: a sympathiser with communists who is not a party member

definitions.text: on the same train as me?
definitions.meaning: taken literally, a companion on a journey by rail

explanation.surface: A football fan wonders whether a stranger heading to the match is backing Liverpool too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Reds' could be a football team, but here they are communists; the question mark flags the literal reading of a fellow passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a political sympathiser with communism and, literally, a companion journeying alongside someone.

clue.text: Squire's way right around county

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece goes about the other

parts.note: a lane is a way or road
Down is a county of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A country gentleman's path goes right round the shire.
explanation.walkthrough: County Down is in Northern Ireland; LANE and R wrap round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A squire is the chief owner of land in an English rural parish.

clue.text: Many cheer, scattering chief foe

indicators.note: scattering means spreading things about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Crowds cheer as the main enemy flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattering' rearranges MANY CHEER.
explanation.definitionFit: One's principal adversary, the greatest of opponents.

clue.text: Unusual kind of eccentric fraud

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters of these words come out in an unexpected new order

explanation.surface: A strange sort of oddball is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges all the letters of KIND OF ECCENTRIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindle in which a trickster first wins the victim's trust is a classic scam.

clue.text: No gas here cooking coq au vin? Without question

indicators.note: cooking means mixing up, so the letters are rearranged
without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether the stove has gas for a chicken in wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without question' removes Q from COQ AU VIN, and 'cooking' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means in a vacuum, a space empty of any gas or matter.

clue.text: Traveller wearing brown drill

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so one piece is wrapped round another

parts.note: tan is a brown colour
a rep is a commercial traveller, a salesman

explanation.surface: A salesman in a brown uniform does his exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' wraps the colour round the salesman; 'drill' is the surgical tool, not practice.
explanation.definitionFit: A trepan is a surgeon's boring tool for cutting into the skull.

clue.text: Husband loves extremely short cleaner

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, and two loves give two O shapes

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, losing the last letter

parts.note: extremely means very

explanation.surface: A man adores a tiny cleaning woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' takes the last letter off VERY to give VER.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoover is a brand of vacuum cleaner, used in Britain for any vacuum.

clue.text: Man in pub falls over? This clearly hasn't worked

indicators.note: something that falls over ends up upside down, which in a down clue reverses it
the clue word that signals this step

parts.note: a bar is a pub
he means a man

explanation.surface: A drunk collapses in a pub, showing that treatment failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' gives BAHER, and 'falls over' reverses it in this down entry. The definition is ironic: a patient back in the pub shows the treatment failed.
explanation.definitionFit: Addiction treatment has evidently failed if the patient is back drinking in a pub.

clue.text: Cross removed from outside, never to be broken?

indicators.note: something removed from a word is taken out of it

parts.note: external means outside
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A cross is taken off the exterior of something meant to stay intact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective but is the letter X, taken out of EXTERNAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting, like an eternal vow, is meant never to end or be broken.

clue.text: Green paper assimilated by church body

indicators.note: assimilated means absorbed, so one piece is taken inside

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
the i is a British newspaper

explanation.surface: An environmental policy document is adopted by a synod.
explanation.walkthrough: The i is a British national daily paper; 'Green' is inexperienced, not ecological.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone green is inexperienced and innocent, lacking worldly wisdom.

clue.text: Go bananas, having been stood up

indicators.note: standing a word up in a down clue turns it from bottom to top

parts.note: bananas and bats both mean crazy

explanation.surface: Someone goes mad after being jilted on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stood up' looks like a date gone wrong, but turns BATS upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a go at something is making an attempt, a try.

clue.text: Old king retired, carrying current coat

indicators.note: carrying means holding something inside
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Cnut, or Canute, was an eleventh-century king of England
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A former monarch in retirement wears a coat that is in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns CNUT into TUNC, which takes I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic is a close-fitting jacket, as in a soldier's uniform tunic.

clue.text: Hear this from ass hacking across English hectares

indicators.note: lying across means spanning the inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: hewing is hacking, as with an axe
HA is the symbol for hectares

explanation.surface: A donkey braying is heard as someone chops through English fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ass' is the animal, not an insult; 'across' sets the two abbreviations inside the word for hacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's bray is the sound one hears from it, so its noise is what an ass makes.

clue.text: Street vendors borrow nuts fed to horses

indicators.note: food fed to an animal goes inside it

parts.note: bays are reddish-brown horses

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters are put in a wild new order

explanation.surface: Market traders take out loans for horse feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' rearranges the borrowing word into RROWBO, and 'fed to' puts that inside the horses. 'nuts' looks like food for the horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders selling fruit and veg from handcarts in the street are a London tradition.

clue.text: Main entrance to top stately home

parts.note: the main is an old word for the sea

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: The chief way in to a grand house is at its top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like 'chief' but is the sea, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: A country seat is an aristocratic family's grand country house.
